candidate.crime: A treasury analyst diverted $84,000 through a fraudulent vendor payment and concealed the transfer in a reconciliation file.
candidate.briefing: You are investigating an $84,000 payment sent from Meridian Bank to a newly added vendor. The treasury analyst says the payment was approved and entered during her shift, but the vendor has no bank account on file. Review the records and question her about the approval timeline.
detective_leads: Vendor file added the day before
Her access card failed at lunch
candidate.suspect_true_story: She created a fake vendor, routed $84,000 to an account she controlled, and altered the reconciliation file to hide it. She initiated the payment before her shift ended, then claimed it had been approved afterward.
candidate.suspect_cover_story: She says the vendor was legitimate and the payment was approved by her manager during her shift. She claims she entered it only after receiving that approval and altered the reconciliation file to correct a routine coding error.
candidate.the_lie: She claims she entered the payment after her manager approved it.
candidate.the_truth: She entered the payment before approval; the approval record was created later, after her manager had left the bank for the day.
candidate.the_contradiction: Ask when she entered the payment, then who approved it and when. The payment timestamp is 4:12 p.m., while her manager's bank access log shows he left at 3:40 p.m.; the approval was recorded at 5:06 p.m.
stress_triggers: Ask why the payment predates approval
Ask who controlled the vendor account
deflection_tactics: Offers to discuss the coding error instead
Says the vendor setup was another team's job
candidate.verbal_tics: Says “just to be clear” before answers; starts giving exact times when nervous.

corpus.criterion: Legitimate vendor conflicts with fake vendor; recorded approval and physical departure do not establish actual authorization time.

candidate.crime: A litigation partner embezzled $84,000 from a client trust account through a false vendor invoice.
candidate.objective: Prove the trust transfer was fraudulent
candidate.briefing: You are investigating a missing $84,000 from a client trust account at Meridian Legal. The transfer was approved using a legitimate vendor’s details, but the vendor says it never received the funds. You will question the firm’s billing manager, who says he only processed a routine payment.
detective_leads: Billing manager says he never called vendor
A partner disputes last quarter’s bonus
candidate.suspect_true_story: He created a false invoice using a real vendor’s account details and routed $84,000 from the client trust account to an account he controlled. He claims he simply processed a payment request, but he had called the vendor to verify the account details and substituted his own account number.
candidate.suspect_cover_story: He says a litigation partner sent him a completed invoice, and he processed it without contacting the vendor or changing any payment details. He claims the funds went to the account listed on the invoice.
candidate.the_lie: He says he never contacted the vendor about the invoice or its payment details.
candidate.the_truth: He called the vendor to confirm the invoice details, then replaced the vendor’s account number with one he controlled.
candidate.the_contradiction: Ask who supplied the vendor’s account details, then press him on the verification call recorded in the firm’s phone log; he says he never called, but the log shows his extension called the vendor before payment, and the vendor recalls he read back the account number.
stress_triggers: Questions about the recorded vendor call
Asking who entered the account number
Mentioning the client trust account audit
deflection_tactics: Blames the partner who approved the invoice
Emphasizes how many payments he handled
Asks whether the vendor’s systems were compromised
Insists the audit procedure was unclear
candidate.verbal_tics: Uses exact dollar amounts when calm; starts saying “to be precise” when cornered.

corpus.criterion: Crime names partner, truth names billing manager; no contact and no payment changes are independent false claims.

candidate.crime: A sealed client escrow account is short by $18,400 after an internal transfer was recorded.
candidate.briefing: You are investigating a shortfall in a sealed client escrow account at Meridian Law. An $18,400 transfer was recorded during the week the account was reconciled. Ask the records clerk about the transfer and test one specific claim in his account.
detective_leads: Escrow transfer has a second-factor trail
candidate.suspect_true_story: Julian Mercer initiated the $18,400 transfer from the escrow account to an outside account using his assigned credentials. He left the office before the transfer completed and later approved it remotely using his registered phone. The firm system requires a separate second-factor approval; a later log entry alone does not establish approval, and leaving the building does not exclude remote access.
candidate.suspect_cover_story: I processed the transfer as part of the reconciliation, and the account was already short when I checked it. I left the office before the transfer completed. I did not approve it remotely after I left.
candidate.the_lie: I did not approve it remotely after I left.
candidate.the_truth: He approved the transfer remotely on his registered phone after leaving the office.
candidate.the_contradiction: If asked to pin down how approval worked, Julian says he had no firm token with him after leaving. The public lead about the second-factor trail points to the escrow audit record; ordinary follow-up questions about the approval method and registered device reveal that the transfer required a one-time code sent to his registered phone, and the audit record shows that code was entered from that phone after his office badge-out time. The system requires this separate approval to complete a transfer
stress_triggers: Whether his registered phone received the approval code
Why he left before the transfer completed
How he knew the account was already short
deflection_tactics: Blames a reconciliation delay without naming evidence
Redirects questions to the client’s late paperwork
Asks whether anyone else had access
candidate.verbal_tics: Says “to be precise” before correcting small details; becomes unusually formal under pressure.

corpus.criterion: Phone attribution lacks exclusive possession or observed actor identity; do not reject merely because of missing final punctuation.

candidate.crime: A scheduled $84,600 supplier payment was diverted to a different bank account before it was released.
candidate.briefing: You are investigating a diverted supplier payment at Meridian Hospital. Interview procurement analyst Ivo Serrano, who says he followed the standard approval process. Identify the false claim in his account; you do not need to prove every element of the crime.
detective_leads: Payment audit shows a quiet revision
candidate.suspect_true_story: Ivo changed the supplier's bank account using a stolen vendor credential, then released the $84,600 payment. He did not have the required second approver's authorization. The payment system records each account revision and approval as separate events, and an approval must be explicitly entered by a second authorized user before release. He left the hospital before the release, but used remote access afterward.
candidate.suspect_cover_story: I changed the supplier's bank account after receiving a vendor update request. The second approver entered his authorization before I released the payment. I left the hospital before the payment was released, and I did not access the system remotely afterward.
candidate.the_lie: The second approver entered his authorization before I released the payment.
candidate.the_truth: Ivo released the payment without a second approver's authorization; the later approval entry was added after release using Ivo's own credentials.
candidate.the_contradiction: The public payment audit shows release at 16:42 and an approval entry at 16:49; system procedure confirms that only an explicit second-user approval entered before release authorizes payment. Follow-up audit records show the 16:49 entry used Ivo's credentials, not the approver's, so the later timestamp is not evidence of earlier approval.
stress_triggers: Who supplied the vendor's new bank details?
Why was the approval entered seven minutes later?
Why does the later entry use his credentials?
How did he access the system after leaving?
deflection_tactics: Recasts the account change as routine paperwork.
Emphasizes that the payment amount matched the invoice.
Insists the audit timestamps are easy to misread.
Asks whether the vendor complaint has been resolved.
candidate.verbal_tics: Uses exact times and says “for the record” before redirecting.

corpus.criterion: Cover denies remote access as well as claiming prior approval; private truth contradicts both.

candidate.crime: A ledger disappeared from the trading office after closing.
candidate.objective: Establish one contradiction, then identify the false claim about returning to the building. Presence alone does not prove theft.
candidate.briefing: A ledger disappeared from a fictional trading office. Ask Casey Vale about the evening, compare the available records, and identify the specific false claim. This is an authored practice case with live AI dialogue.
detective_leads: Compare the departure claim with the visitor record.
Check whose name appears on each record.
candidate.suspect_cover_story: I left at six and did not return to the building that evening.
candidate.suspect_true_story: Casey returned to the building at 18:42. The visitor record establishes presence, not who took the ledger.
candidate.the_lie: I left at six and did not return to the building that evening.
candidate.the_truth: Casey returned to the building at 18:42. The visitor record establishes presence, not who took the ledger.
candidate.the_contradiction: The statement says there was no return after six, but the visitor record names Casey arriving at 18:42. These accounts conflict about returning to the building.
stress_triggers: The difference between presence and responsibility
deflection_tactics: Question the accuracy of the time
Point to the unrelated badge record
candidate.verbal_tics: Precise about work, evasive about times.

corpus.criterion: The existing authored visitor record contradicts absence; neither goal nor proof claims theft.

candidate.crime: A file was moved between office drawers.
candidate.briefing: Ask Ari about moving the file. The desk observer and timestamped video are available facts to discuss.
detective_leads: Compare the account with the desk observation.
candidate.suspect_cover_story: I worked at the desk that afternoon. I never moved the file.
candidate.suspect_true_story: Ari worked at the desk that afternoon and moved the file from drawer A to drawer B at 14:10. The observer knew Ari personally, saw Ari move it and confirmed Ari on the timestamped video. Moving the file does not establish theft.
candidate.the_truth: Ari moved the file from drawer A to drawer B at 14:10.
candidate.the_contradiction: The desk observer personally recognized Ari moving the file at 14:10; timestamped video confirms the same action. Ask Ari about that observation. This establishes movement, not theft.

corpus.criterion: One false movement claim; personally recognized eyewitness and confirming video explicitly bind the action to Ari; no theft inference.

limits: Six existing fictional cases, same-model independent prompt, not human review or statistical reliability.

singleFalseClaim.reason: The designated lie is “entered the payment after her manager approved it.” The true story says she “entered the payment before approval”; the separate legitimacy and coding-error claims are not independently contradicted by the stated truth.

canonicalConsistency.reason: The role “Treasury Analyst” is consistent with the true story, and the timeline—manager left at “3:40 p.m.,” payment at “4:12 p.m.,” approval recorded at “5:06 p.m.”—supports entry before recorded approval. No required-system workflow is specified.

evidenceSufficiency.reason: The “payment timestamp is 4:12 p.m.” and approval was “recorded at 5:06 p.m.” establish ordering, but the stated facts do not establish when she actually entered the payment; the private truth alone cannot supply that missing link.

publicDiscoverability.reason: The lead “Reconciliation saved before approval logged” and briefing prompt about the “approval timeline” suggest questioning, but the suspect's stated facts do not say when she entered it or what she knows about the entry timestamp; the essential revelation is unsupported.

completeReasoning.reason: The contradiction is a complete sentence and clearly contrasts “4:12 p.m.” with “5:06 p.m.” and the manager leaving at “3:40 p.m.”; however, that ordering does not itself resolve who entered the payment when.

singleFalseClaim.reason: The designated lie is the no-contact claim ("never contacted the vendor"); the remaining cover statements about the partner sending a completed invoice and the funds going to the listed account are not independently contradicted by the stated true story.

canonicalConsistency.reason: The suspect is consistently the billing manager, and the true story aligns with his role. No required-system workflow or chronology is contradicted; the partner's alleged approval is presented as cover, not canonical fact.

evidenceSufficiency.reason: The phone log and vendor recollection link a call to the suspect ("his extension called the vendor"; "vendor recalls he read back the account number"), but neither establishes that the account number he read back was the substituted account he controlled. The necessary identity/account link is missing.

publicDiscoverability.reason: The lead that the manager "never called vendor" and the stated phone log give an ordinary questioning path; the contradiction says the vendor recalls the call and read-back, and suspect can discuss those records.

completeReasoning.reason: The contradiction is a complete no-contact rebuttal: it identifies the call log, places the call before payment, and states the vendor recalls the number read-back.

singleFalseClaim.reason: The designated lie, “I did not approve it remotely after I left,” is contradicted by the true story that he “later approved it remotely.” The other material cover statements—that he processed the transfer during reconciliation, the account was already short, and he left before completion—are not independently contradicted by the supplied truth.

canonicalConsistency.reason: The true story says Julian “initiated the $18,400 transfer” and “later approved it remotely”; the contradiction explains the required separate second-factor step and says the audit records approval after “office badge-out time.” The transfer workflow and role are consistent; no conflicting canonical identity, role, or chronology is stated.

evidenceSufficiency.reason: The audit record links code entry to his registered phone after badge-out, but the evidence does not establish that Julian possessed or used that phone at that time. A registered device alone does not identify its user; the private truth asserts remote approval but the stated public evidence lacks the necessary attribution link.

publicDiscoverability.reason: The lead “Escrow transfer has a second-factor trail” provides a plausible questioning path, and the contradiction states that ordinary follow-up questions reveal the code method, registered device, and audit timing. However, that path does not supply the missing proof that Julian himself used the phone.

completeReasoning.reason: The contradiction ends with the cut-off sentence “The system requires this separate approval to complete a transfer”; it is incomplete. It also leaves unstated the essential link from phone use to Julian personally.

singleFalseClaim.reason: The designated lie is contradicted by the truth, but the cover story also says “I did not access the system remotely afterward,” while suspect_true_story says he “used remote access afterward”—a second independent falsehood.

canonicalConsistency.reason: suspect_role is “Procurement Analyst,” consistent with suspect_true_story; the later approval is a separate event, and suspect_true_story explicitly explains remote access after leaving. No conflicting canonical identity, role, or workflow is stated.

evidenceSufficiency.reason: the_contradiction gives release at “16:42” and approval at “16:49,” plus the rule that approval must be “entered before release,” directly refuting prior approval. But suspect_true_story says the later entry used Ivo’s credentials, and the stated evidence gives no link showing Ivo personally used them; the rules also require a second authorized user, while “using Ivo's credentials” alone does not establish who entered the record.

publicDiscoverability.reason: detective_leads mentions “Payment audit shows a quiet revision,” but the candidate does not state that the public briefing or leads expose the release/approval timestamps or the before-release rule. The_contradiction supplies them privately, without stating a public questioning path or facts Ivo can reveal.

completeReasoning.reason: the_contradiction states both exact times and the required ordering rule, so the core contradiction is complete and intelligible; it is not cut off.

singleFalseClaim.reason: The designated claim is “I left at six and did not return to the building that evening”; the true story says “Casey returned to the building at 18:42.” No other material cover statement is supplied.

canonicalConsistency.reason: The identity and role are consistent: “Casey Vale” is the suspect and “Operations analyst.” The chronology agrees that Casey “returned to the building at 18:42”; no conflicting workflow or capability is described.

The briefing mentions “available records” without specifying their contents or linking the record to Casey.

publicDiscoverability.reason: The lead to “Compare the departure claim with the visitor record” gives a plausible path, but the briefing does not state the visitor record’s 18:42 entry or that it names Casey; the required public evidence is missing.

completeReasoning.reason: The reasoning is complete: the claim says “did not return” after leaving at six, while the contradiction gives a return “at 18:42.” No cutoff or additional inference is needed in the stated contradiction.
